items.title: Adversity and Blessing
items.moral: Moral: A hardship that brings you closer to Allah is a blessing, while a blessing that draws you away from Him becomes a hardship. What matters is where it leads you, not how comfortable it makes you.
body: If adversity brings you closer to Allah, it is a blessing.
If a blessing draws you away from Allah, it is a hardship.

items.title: Neither Gossip nor Dust
items.moral: Moral: Protect both your reputation and your dignity. Do not give people reason to gossip about you, and do not allow anyone to treat you without respect.
body: “A tale on every tongue” means being the subject of gossip, rumors, or constant public discussion.
“Dust beneath anyone’s feet” means allowing others to humiliate, belittle, or treat you as worthless.

items.title: Everyone Has Work to Do
items.moral: Moral: It is a very painful feeling to live knowing you are regarded as unreliable and untrustworthy.
body: I have been fortunate to learn from wise teachers. One was my literature teacher, the esteemed Baladadash. He taught us never to leave a request or an assigned task unanswered, however small it might seem.

Everyone has things to do. When someone asks for help, it is usually because they need you, not because they have nothing better to do. Do not leave them waiting in silence. If you cannot help, say so openly. Failing to answer erodes their trust.

items.title: A Fly in a China Shop
items.moral: Moral: A small lie whispered into an ignorant ear can cause enormous destruction. Knowledge, critical thinking, and strong moral values are our best protection against it.
body: A fly could never wreck a china shop on its own. But if it flew into a bull’s ear, the panicked animal could destroy the whole place.
The fly represents superstition, falsehood, and prejudice. The bull represents an ignorant person who acts without thinking.

items.title: The Fortieth Day
items.moral: Moral: Customs can hold generations of love and blessings. A baby’s gifts express hopes for an entire lifetime.
body: In some Turkic communities, tradition keeps a mother and newborn at home without visitors for forty days after the birth. The custom is said to date back to the Göktürks.

On the fortieth day, a close relative invites the mother and baby to visit and presents symbolic gifts: coins for prosperity; cotton for a long life and a gentle heart, even when the child’s hair turns white; sugar for sweet words and a cheerful face; wheat for abundance at home; salt for a life that never loses its flavor; and eggs for nourishment and strength.
